How CAPTCHAs work, and why they keep getting harder

Most people meet a CAPTCHA as a box that says "I'm not a robot", or a grid of blurry crosswalks, or a page that asks them to verify you are human before it lets them read anything. The name stands for Completely Automated Public Turing test to tell Computers and Humans Apart, and the idea is older than most of the sites that use it: give the visitor a task that a person finds easy and a program finds hard, and let only the people through.

The first generation used distorted text. A server drew a word, bent the letters, added lines and noise, and asked the visitor to type what they saw. For a few years that worked, because optical character recognition was poor at reading warped text. It stopped working once recognition models improved, and by the middle of the 2010s software could read the distorted words more reliably than people could. The puzzles that were left were the ones people failed most often.

The second generation moved the test from the visitor's eyes to the visitor's behaviour. Google's reCAPTCHA in its checkbox form watches how the mouse moves toward the box, how long the page has been open, what cookies the browser carries and whether the same browser has passed before. Most visitors click once and never see a puzzle. The image grid only appears when the score is uncertain, which is why some people see it every time and others never do.

The third generation tries to remove the visible test altogether. Cloudflare's Turnstile, hCaptcha's passive mode and the bot managers sold by companies such as PerimeterX, DataDome and Akamai run small programs in the page that measure the browser itself: the fonts it reports, how it renders a hidden canvas, how quickly it answers a proof of work, whether its claimed screen size matches its window. A visitor who passes sees nothing more than a short interstitial. A visitor who fails sees a press and hold button, a puzzle, or a page that says they have been blocked.

Each step raises the cost for automated traffic, and each step also raises the cost for ordinary people who look unusual to the scoring model. Screen reader users, people on shared networks, people who clear their cookies and people in countries with less common browser setups all fail more often. Audio alternatives exist, but they are often harder than the visual test they replace. The accessibility complaints have been steady for twenty years and the tests have not become easier.

There is also an economic side. Services that solve CAPTCHAs for a fee have existed for almost as long as the tests, first with people in low-wage markets typing answers by hand and later with models that solve the common puzzle types directly. The price for a thousand solved image puzzles has fallen to a few dollars. That has pushed site owners toward the behavioural and device checks, which are harder to buy answers for, and away from puzzles that only test whether someone can see.

For a reader, the practical upshot is simple. A page that shows only a checkbox, a spinner and a line asking you to wait is almost always a check of the browser, not of the person. Waiting a few seconds, keeping cookies enabled and avoiding unusual browser extensions clears most of them. The pages that still refuse are usually making a decision about the network the request came from, and no amount of clicking on traffic lights changes that.

Measuring whether any of this works is harder than it sounds. A site can count how many visitors were stopped, but it cannot easily count how many of them were people who gave up and left. Vendors publish detection rates measured against their own test traffic, and those numbers rarely include the false positives that matter most to the site owner: paying customers who were turned away on a busy day. The honest metric is the share of real visitors who reached the page they asked for, and few sites collect it.

Logged-in visitors are a special case. A site that already knows who a visitor is has less reason to test them, and many sites quietly skip the check for accounts in good standing. That is one reason the same page can feel open in one browser and closed in another: the first browser carries a session cookie from a login weeks ago, and the second does not. Clearing cookies resets that history, which is why the advice to keep cookies enabled appears on so many challenge pages.

Tools that read pages on someone's behalf, such as feed readers, archivers and research assistants, sit in the middle of this. They are automated by definition, yet they act for a person who could have opened the page themselves. Some sites publish feeds or offer an official interface for exactly this kind of reader. Others treat every automated request the same way, and the reader ends up holding a challenge page instead of the article it was asked to fetch.

For the people who build these systems, the open question is how long the device checks will hold. Every signal they read can in principle be imitated by a careful enough browser, and the history of the field is a history of signals that worked until they were imitated. The likely result is not a final test but a continuing negotiation, with each side paying a little more every year to stay where it is.
